stories.title: What Chicago built, and what it cleared
stories.dek: Eight places where fire-insurance surveyors drew a complete neighbourhood, and something later took its place. Drag the divider at each stop.

stops.title: A highway needs a hundred blocks
stops.body_html:
On the left, the 1917 survey of the Near West Side: solid block after solid block, buildings on both sides of every street, right across the middle of the frame.

On the right, the same ground. The Eisenhower and Congress Parkway run straight through it. Nothing on the left thinned out gradually — a line was drawn and everything inside it was taken.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1917, Vol. 7 (Library of Congress)

stops.title: The same corridor, a generation earlier
stops.body_html:
Two miles west, and back to the 1890s sheets — a different survey of the same corridor, twenty-five years before the one you just looked at.

The blocks were already complete then. The point of showing both is that this was not a district in decline that a highway happened to finish off. It was built, and it stayed built, until it was removed.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1896, Vols. 11-12 (Library of Congress)

stops.title: The Kennedy, through Logan Square
stops.body_html:
The 1921 sheets draw two-flats and cottages on a complete grid, with a rail line running north-west on the diagonal.

On the right, that diagonal is the Kennedy Expressway. The route was not chosen through empty ground — it widened a rail corridor, and the blocks on either side of it went.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1921, Vol. 10 (Library of Congress)

stops.title: The Dan Ryan, past the ballpark
stops.body_html:
The 1912 sheets draw an ordinary street grid here, with the old Comiskey Park grandstand at the bottom of the frame — a ballpark set into a neighbourhood, on a normal block.

On the right, at the same scale, the Dan Ryan: express lanes, local lanes and frontage roads together, wider than any block on the left. The grid did not shrink to make room for it. It was removed.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1912, Vol. 4 (Library of Congress)

stops.title: The Dan Ryan, through Englewood
stops.body_html:
The 1895 survey of Englewood. Almost every building on these blocks is drawn yellow — frame construction: small, cheap, built one at a time by people who could afford one at a time. Block after block of it, with no gaps.

On the right, the Dan Ryan and the Chicago Skyway split apart across the same ground. This is the oldest survey in the story and the most complete neighbourhood in it.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1895, Vol. 15 (Library of Congress)

stops.title: Where the highways meet, and the campus that followed
stops.body_html:
The eastern end of the same corridor, and a different kind of clearance. On the right three expressways converge in the Circle Interchange, and beside it sits the university superblock built on the blocks the atlas is still drawing.

The comparison worth making is not old buildings against new ones. It is the grain — how many separate owners, how many front doors, how many ways through, per acre. That is the quantity the left pane has and the right pane does not.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1917, Vol. 7 (Library of Congress)

stops.title: The parking around the United Center
stops.body_html:
This is the ground the 1901 Project proposes to build on. The atlas shows what was there before it became surface parking: a complete fine-grained grid, block after block of it.

The argument this supports is not that the old blocks should be recreated exactly. It is that this land carried a walkable neighbourhood within living memory, so the question for a megaproject here is whether it puts that grain back or replaces one single-use superblock with another.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1917, Vol. 7 (Library of Congress)
Strong Towns Chicago — 3 ways to make this Chicago megaproject a success for everyone

stops.title: Giles Avenue, 31st to 35th
stops.body_html:
Not every clearance was for a road. On the left, the 1912 sheets draw unbroken rowhouse blocks; on the right, towers standing in open ground.

The change is not density — the buildings on the right hold people too. It is the street. On the left every building meets a sidewalk; on the right most of the ground is neither building nor street, and there is nothing to walk to.

sources.label: Sanborn atlas, Chicago 1912, Vol. 4 (Library of Congress)
